canonical_statement: The authors reviewed their recent heparin-treated deep venous thrombosis experience to identify factors that might influence treatment results and treatment risks.
The study reviewed inpatient records of patients diagnosed with deep venous thrombosis at the University of California, Davis Medical Center during 1977 and 1978.

Patients with active, clinically apparent deep venous thrombosis treated with heparin were included; asymptomatic deep venous thrombosis and thrombosis due to malignant venous obstruction were excluded.

population.label: Heparin-treated patients with active clinically apparent deep venous thrombosis
inclusion_criteria: Active, clinically apparent deep venous thrombosis
exclusion_criteria: Thrombosis due to malignant venous obstruction

canonical_statement: The hospital-recommended heparin regimen was reported as an intravenous loading dose of 50 units/kg/hour followed by continuous intravenous infusion at 25 units/kg/hour, adjusted to an ACT target of 150 to 210 seconds.

exposures.details: Source reports a preceding loading dose of 50 units/kg/hour; dose was adjusted to ACT 150-210 seconds.

canonical_statement: The cohort comprised 121 patients with 156 episodes of deep venous thrombosis; 75 patients were men and 46 were women, ages 17 to 80 years with an average age of 50 years.
Multiple deep venous thrombosis episodes occurred in 20% of patients during the study period.
Previous deep venous thrombosis was the most common predisposing condition, present in 73 patients (47%).
Medical illness was reported as a predisposing factor in 16 patients (10%).
An abdominal, orthopedic, thoracic, or neurosurgical operation 3 days to 4 months before deep venous thrombosis was reported in 27 patients (17%).
Leg or pelvic trauma was reported as a predisposing factor in 16 patients (10%).
Multisystem trauma was reported as a predisposing factor in 6 patients (4%).
Other venous diseases were reported as a predisposing factor in 4 patients (3%).
Oral contraceptive use was reported as a predisposing factor in 1 patient (0.6%).
No predisposing condition was identified in 12 patients (8%).
The clinical diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis was supported by objective diagnostic methods in 71% of cases.

Objective diagnostic methods included phlebography in 49% of cases, iodine-123-fibrinogen scanning in 19%, Doppler examination in 1%, and autopsy confirmation in 1%; three additional patients with pulmonary symptoms had pulmonary embolism documented by ventilation-perfusion scanning.
Heparin treatment was delivered by continuous intravenous infusion in 153 cases, intermittent intravenous administration in 1 case, and full-dose subcutaneous administration in 2 cases.
Heparin treatment was monitored with ACT in 146 cases, partial thromboplastin time in 5 cases, and no coagulation test in 5 cases.
The heparin dose averaged 21 units/kg/hour; among patients whose average ACT was 150 to 210 seconds, doses ranged from 9 to 39 units/kg/hour.

exposures.details: Average dose; range 9-39 units/kg/hour among patients with average ACT 150-210 seconds.

canonical_statement: Average ACT was within the target range in 103 patients, above target in 8, and below target in 35.

population.label: Heparin-treated DVT cases with reported ACT category

canonical_statement: Heparin therapy lasted 1 to 31 days (average 9 days); warfarin was begun in 63% of cases between heparin days 1 and 5, and outpatient warfarin was continued for 3 to 6 months when used.

exposures.details: Started in 63% of cases between days 1 and 5 of heparin therapy.

canonical_statement: A delayed response was defined as requiring 7 or more days of heparin therapy before significant pain relief was documented.

outcome.definition: Seven or more days of heparin therapy required before significant relief of pain was described in the chart.

canonical_statement: Treatment failure was defined as recurrent deep venous thrombosis during heparin therapy, pulmonary embolism during heparin therapy, or failure of pain to resolve after a heparin course lasting at least 1 week.

outcome.definition: Recurrent DVT during heparin therapy, pulmonary embolism during heparin therapy, or unresolved pain after at least 1 week of heparin.

canonical_statement: No delayed responses occurred among 33 patients with average ACT at least 180 seconds, whereas 4 of 65 patients (6.2%) with average ACT below 180 seconds had a delayed response.

population.label: Objectively confirmed DVT cases evaluated for treatment response

outcome.definition: Seven or more days to significant pain relief

canonical_statement: No treatment failures occurred among 33 patients with average ACT at least 180 seconds, whereas 7 of 65 patients (10.8%) with average ACT below 180 seconds had treatment failure.

population.label: Objectively confirmed DVT cases evaluated for treatment response

outcome.definition: Recurrent DVT, pulmonary embolism, or unresolved pain after >=1 week

canonical_statement: Patients with average ACT below 180 seconds required a mean 3.1 days to respond, compared with 2.0 days for patients with ACT at least 180 seconds; the difference was significant at p<0.05.

canonical_statement: Major or minor bleeding, including an unexplained hematocrit decrease of at least 5 points, occurred in 43 of 156 cases (27%).

outcome.definition: Major or minor bleeding, including unexplained hematocrit decrease >=5 points

canonical_statement: Minor bleeding occurred in 33 of 156 cases (21%).

outcome.definition: Bleeding not requiring transfusion or other specific therapy and not endangering life or producing sequelae

canonical_statement: Major bleeding occurred in 10 of 156 cases (6%); nine patients required transfusion and one had a cerebrovascular accident, and no patient died as a result of anticoagulation.

outcome.definition: Life-threatening bleeding or bleeding requiring transfusion

canonical_statement: Heparin therapy was discontinued prematurely in 9 patients because of bleeding.

concept.text: Premature heparin discontinuation due to bleeding

canonical_statement: Minor bleeding occurred in 17 of 43 cases (40%) with ACT at least 180 seconds versus 16 of 113 cases (14%) with ACT below 180 seconds; this difference was significant at the 0.05 level.

canonical_statement: Major bleeding occurred in 3 of 43 cases (7%) with ACT at least 180 seconds versus 7 of 113 cases (6%) with ACT below 180 seconds; the authors reported no increase in major bleeding with ACT at least 180 seconds.

canonical_statement: Two patients were noted to have thrombocytopenia of no clinical consequence while receiving heparin; a third patient’s thrombocytopenia was attributed to chemotherapy, and no bleeding episode was attributed to thrombocytopenia.
Platelet counts were infrequently monitored after heparin therapy was begun.
Clinically manifested pulmonary embolism during heparin therapy occurred in 1 of 156 DVT episodes in the series.
Recurrent deep venous thrombosis during heparin therapy occurred in 1 of 156 DVT episodes in the series.

concept.text: Recurrent deep venous thrombosis during heparin therapy

canonical_statement: The study did not specifically evaluate long-term outcomes.

canonical_statement: For most patients with established deep venous thrombosis, the authors favored an aggressive heparin regimen maintaining ACT above 180 seconds and increasing heparin dose if symptoms persisted.

canonical_statement: The authors advocated higher doses of heparin for most patients with deep venous thrombosis because they interpreted their data as showing more rapid and complete recovery.

The authors reported that a prospective controlled long-term study was underway using a high-dose regimen described as a heparin bolus of 300 units/kg/hour followed by 40 units/kg/hour for 72 hours and then conventional doses.

exposures.details: Planned study regimen; source reports a preceding bolus of 300 units/kg/hour, followed by conventional doses after 72 hours.
